results.blind_working: Frequency does not change on refraction. Wavelength in glass = 600/1.5 = 400 nm.
Each layer contributes thickness/n. Water: 12/(4/3) = 9 cm. Liquid: 9/1.5 = 6 cm. Total apparent depth = 15 cm.

A true: speed and wavelength both drop by a factor of n. B false: normal shift t(1 - 1/n) does not depend on object distance. C true: parallel faces give lateral displacement with no deviation. D true: the fish sees the object n times farther. E false: R is positive when the centre of curvature is on the refracted-light side.
u = -10, f = 15: 1/v = 1/15 - 1/10 = -1/30, so v = -30 cm (same side as object, virtual). m = v/u = +3.
A is true: n_lens/n_liquid < 1 makes the convex lens diverge. R is true: n is larger for violet, so f is shorter. R is about dispersion, so it does not explain A.
I: f = R/(n-1) = 15/0.5 = 30 cm, so I is correct. II: cutting perpendicular to the axis gives two plano-convex halves, each with f = 40 cm, so II is incorrect.
Light emerges only where incidence is below the critical angle, so r = h tan C = h/sqrt(n^2-1) = 8/sqrt(25/9-1) = 8/(4/3) = 6 cm.
TIR at 45° needs C < 45°, so sin45° > 1/n, giving n > √2 ≈ 1.414. Only 1.50 qualifies.

Diamond: small critical angle 24.4° (III). Optical fibre: core denser than cladding (I). Mirage: TIR at hot rarer air near the ground (IV). Periscope prism: right-angled isosceles prism with n > √2 (II).
A true. B true, since violet has larger n and so smaller C. C false, since TIR transmits no refracted light. D false, since glass-water has a smaller relative n and so a larger C. E true.
For a concave lens f = -25 cm = -0.25 m, so P = 1/f = -4 D.
Take u = -30 cm and f = +20 cm. Then 1/v = 1/20 - 1/30 = 1/60, so v = +60 cm. m = v/u = -2, so the image is real and inverted.
In air the lens factor is (1.5 - 1) = 0.5. In water it is (1.5/(4/3) - 1) = 0.125, so power scales by 0.125/0.5 = 1/4. P becomes 5/4 = +1.25 D (taking P = 1/f, the usual NEET convention).

A is true: a concave lens always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image of a real object. R is also true. However, the sign of the power alone does not explain the image characteristics, so R is not the correct explanation of A.
I: a real image from a single lens is inverted, and area magnification = m^2 = 9, so I is correct. II: f = +20 cm and u = -15 cm give v = -60 cm. Then m = +4, not +2, so II is incorrect.
Lens f = 20 cm (P = 5 D); mirror f = 10 cm (P = 10 D). P = 2(5) + 10 = 20 D, so f = 5 cm.
A true. B false: magnifications multiply. C true: net power 0. D true: virtual object with u positive in the Cartesian convention. E false: 1/F = 1/20 + 1/20 - 40/400 = 0, so F is infinite.

R is true: the thin-prism formula δ = (n−1)A holds for small angles of incidence. A is false: δ in that regime is essentially independent of incidence angle. In general, deviation first decreases to a minimum and then increases, so it does not rise steadily.
I: at minimum deviation r = A/2 = 30°, not 60°, so I is false. II: emergence requires r2 ≤ C, and since r1 ≤ C, A = r1 + r2 can be at most 2C = 80°. Here A = 85° > 80°, so no ray emerges; II is true.
For a simple microscope with the image at the near point, M = 1 + D/f = 1 + 25/5 = 6.
With the final image at infinity, M = (L/f_o)(D/f_e) = (20/2)(25/5) = 10 × 5 = 50.
With the final image at the near point, M = (f_o/f_e)(1 + f_e/D) = 10 × (1 + 5/25) = 10 × 1.2 = 12.

Simple microscope at near point: 1 + D/f (A-III). Simple microscope at infinity: D/f (B-I). Telescope in normal adjustment: f_o/f_e (C-IV). Compound microscope in normal adjustment: (L/f_o)(D/f_e) (D-II).

A is true: both focal lengths are small with f_o < f_e. B is true: a large f_o and large aperture are needed. C is false: the final image is inverted. D is true: mirrors cause no chromatic aberration. E is false: since M = f_o/f_e, a larger f_e decreases M. So A, B and D are correct.
A line source such as a slit produces wavefronts that are cylindrical.
For a line source, intensity is proportional to 1/r. Going from 2 m to 8 m multiplies r by 4, so the intensity becomes I/4.
Speed in glass v = c/n = 3e8/1.5 = 2e8 m/s. Radius r = v t = 2e8 × 2e-9 = 0.4 m = 40 cm.
A is true: at a huge distance the spherical wavefront is effectively plane, so the rays are parallel. R is false: rays are perpendicular to the wavefront, not parallel to it.

Statement I correctly describes Huygens' construction. Statement II is correct: a spherical wave has intensity proportional to 1/r^2, giving 1/4 when r doubles; a cylindrical wave has intensity proportional to 1/r, giving 1/2.
Frequency is set by the source and stays the same at a boundary. Speed and wavelength change, and direction changes for oblique incidence.
lambda_medium = lambda_air / n = 600 / 1.5 = 400 nm.
sin i / sin r = v1/v2 = sqrt3, so sin r = (sqrt3/2)/sqrt3 = 1/2, giving r = 30 degrees.

A: sin i/sin r = v1/v2 (III). B: lambda2 = lambda1 n1/n2 (II). C: frequency is unchanged (I). D: corpuscular theory predicts a greater speed in the denser medium (IV). This matches A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV.

A is true: light bends toward the normal when it slows. B is true: equal wavelet distances in equal times give i = r. C is false: sin i/sin r = n2/n1, not n1/n2. D is false: reflection changes neither wavelength nor frequency. E is true: Huygens' construction explains TIR and the critical angle. So A, B and E only.
Fringe width β = λD/d = (500e-9 × 1)/(0.5e-3) = 1e-3 m = 1 mm.
In water the wavelength becomes λ/μ, so β' = β/μ = 0.6/(4/3) = 0.45 mm.
Shift = (μ-1)tD/d = 0.5 × 10e-6 × 1/1e-3 = 5 mm. The pattern moves towards the covered slit.
Fringe width is λD/d, which the film does not change, so A is true. The pattern shifts towards the covered slit, not away from it, so R is false.
I: phase = 2π/3, so I = 4I0cos²(π/3) = I0 = Imax/4, which is correct. II: amplitude ratio is 3:1, so Imax/Imin = (4/2)² = 4:1, which is correct.
Coherent sources must have the same frequency and a constant (time-independent) phase difference.
Independent lamps are incoherent, so their intensities simply add: I + 4I = 5I.
YDSE uses division of wavefront (A-II). A thin oil film uses division of amplitude (B-I). Independent lamps are incoherent, so intensities add (C-III). A laser is highly coherent (D-IV).

A is true. B is true, since I_min = (√I1 − √I2)² = 0 for equal amplitudes. C is false, because a biprism divides the wavefront. D is true; it follows NCERT's statement that the phase changes about every 10^-10 s. E is false, because narrow, closely spaced slits are needed.
The central maximum width is 2λD/a = 2 × 600e-9 × 1 / 0.2e-3 = 6e-3 m, which is 6 mm.
In the liquid, λ' = λ/(4/3) = 3λ/4. The width is proportional to λ, so it becomes 4.0 × 3/4 = 3.0 mm.
For the second minimum, a sinθ = 2λ. So a = 2 × 600 nm / sin30° = 1200 nm / 0.5 = 2.4 μm.
A is true because the width is 2λD/a, so a narrower slit gives a wider maximum. R is true, since secondary maxima fall off in intensity with order. R does not explain A.
Fresnel distance z = a²/λ = (1e-3)² / 5e-7 = 2 m, so I is correct. Doubling both gives (2a)²/(2λ) = 2a²/λ, which doubles z, so II is incorrect.
Brewster's law: tan i = n = √3, so i = 60°.
The first polaroid passes I0/2. Malus's law at the second gives (I0/2)cos²30° = (I0/2)(3/4) = 3I0/8.
At the Brewster angle i + r = 90°, so i = 90° − 37° = 53°. Then n = tan 53° = 4/3.
A: one polaroid gives I0/2 (III). B: crossed polaroids give 0 (II). C: (I0/2)cos²45° = I0/4 (IV). D: (I0/2)(1/2)(1/2) = I0/8 (I).

A is true (sound is longitudinal). B is true (vibrations are perpendicular to the plane of incidence). C is false: tan⁻¹1.5 ≈ 56.3°. D is true. E is false: the transmitted intensity stays I0/2 at all orientations. So A, B and D only.
Light reflected from a horizontal wet road is partly polarized with its electric vector horizontal. Polaroid sunglasses with a vertical pass axis block this component.
The molecular chains absorb the E-field component parallel to them. The transmitted E vector is therefore perpendicular to the chains.
The first sheet passes 800/2 = 400 W/m^2. Malus's law gives 400 cos^2θ = 100, so cos^2θ = 1/4 and θ = 60°.
Both statements are true applications of polarization. Photoelasticity does not explain how 3D movies work.
I is false: unpolarized light through a rotating single Polaroid gives a constant I0/2. II is false: reflected glare is polarized horizontally, not vertically.
